sections.html:
Indiana Code 32-31-1-20 bars cities, towns and counties from regulating private rental housing unless a state statute authorizes it. A landlord selling a rental in Fort Wayne therefore works from the same statewide framework as one in Evansville.

The section lists what a local government cannot control without state permission:

  • Rental rates, whether set through zoning or any other means.
  • Tenant screening and lease applications.
  • Security deposits and landlord fees.
  • Lease terms and conditions.
  • Required disclosures about the property, the lease or the parties' rights and duties.

A local rule that crosses those lines is void and unenforceable. One exception covers privately owned housing that receives government funds or benefits to offer reduced rents to low or moderate income tenants. For an ordinary rental house, the state code in Title 32, Article 31 is where you look first.

sections.h2: How much notice ends a tenancy?
sections.html:
The notice period depends on the type of tenancy and the reason. A lease can change the defaults. Where the lease is silent, the statute sets these periods.

SituationNotice required
Rent not paid when due (IC 32-31-1-6)At least 10 days; the tenant can stop it by paying in full within the period
Rental of three months or less that renews automatically (IC 32-31-1-4)Notice equal to one rental period
Year-to-year tenancy (IC 32-31-1-3)At least three months before the tenancy year ends
Landlord changes the rental agreement (IC 32-31-5-4)At least 30 days in writing, unless a written agreement says otherwise

Notice is where many sellers get stuck. A house advertised as vacant at closing usually needs a tenancy that has already ended the way the statute and the lease require. Work backward from your target closing date and count the notice period before you set it.

sections.h2: The eviction case step by step
sections.html:
An eviction is a court case, and a landlord cannot skip it. The process runs in two parts: a possession hearing first, then a damages hearing that often comes later.

  • Notice. For nonpayment or another lease violation, the landlord generally gives at least ten days' notice. A tenant who pays in full or fixes the problem in that time cannot be removed on that notice.
  • Service. The tenant receives a complaint, a notice of claim and a summons between 5 and 20 days before the court date, usually delivered by the county sheriff.
  • Possession hearing. The court decides whether the tenant must move. In the common final outcome for nonpayment, the court sets a move-out date, typically two to three weeks away.
  • Immediate possession. A landlord can regain the unit soon after the hearing by paying money into court as a bond in case the eviction was wrong. The tenant can pay the same amount to stay until the damages decision.
  • Damages hearing. The court can award back rent, utilities, property damage and fees to the landlord, or overpaid rent and repair costs to the tenant, within a $10,000 small claims limit.

After an eviction order, a motion to correct error or an appeal is due within 30 days. A tenant who misses the hearing and gets a default judgment may ask to vacate it for good cause within one year. Cases can be looked up at mycase.in.gov.

Tenants in Indiana cannot withhold rent, which is worth remembering when a tenant raises repair complaints before a sale.

sections.h2: What a landlord cannot do while preparing to sell
sections.html:
Locking out a tenant or cutting off essential services is off limits, even when the goal is a vacant house for a quick sale. Under IC 32-31-5-6, unless a court orders otherwise, a landlord may not block access to or possession of the unit. The section lists changing locks, adding a device that keeps the tenant out, and removing doors, windows, fixtures or appliances.

It also bars interrupting or shutting off electricity, gas, water or other essential services. Exceptions cover emergencies, good-faith repairs and necessary construction. The protections stop when a unit is abandoned, meaning the tenant failed to pay or offer rent due and the circumstances would lead a reasonable person to conclude the unit was surrendered. A rental agreement cannot define abandonment differently.

Showing the house to buyers

Showings are allowed with limits. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for inspections, repairs, supplying services or showing the unit to buyers, lenders, prospective tenants, workers or contractors. The landlord in return gives reasonable notice, written or oral, enters at reasonable times and does not use the right of entry to harass the tenant. No notice is needed in an emergency that threatens occupants or the property, or when entry follows a court order.

If your listing agent schedules buyer visits, pass along the same notice standard. A missed courtesy can become a dispute that delays closing.

sections.h2: Tenants and rent when a landlord sells
sections.html:
The sale is valid without the tenant's agreement. Indiana Code 32-31-1-10 says a landlord's conveyance is effective without the attornment of the tenant, so the tenant does not have to accept the new owner for the transfer to count.

One rule settles who gets the rent. If a tenant pays the original landlord before learning of the sale, that payment binds the new owner. Once the tenant has notice, the statute offers no such protection for later payments. Telling tenants in writing as soon as the sale closes, and naming the new payee, closes that gap.

Deposits have their own section, IC 32-31-3-19, covering the sale of property and liability for deposits. Chapter 3 also contains sections on return of deposits, notice of damages, remittance of the full deposit and liability for withheld deposits. Read the whole chapter and keep a ledger for every tenant.

sections.h2: Disclosures a landlord owes a tenant
sections.html:
Indiana asks a landlord to put several things in writing, and some bind whoever buys the property next. A new owner who takes over a rental inherits the duty to keep them current.

  • Manager and agent. At or before the start of the rental agreement, the landlord or a person signing for the landlord must give the tenant the name and address of an Indiana resident manager and an Indiana resident agent who is reasonably accessible and can accept legal papers and notices. One person can fill both roles. The duty binds any successor landlord, owner or manager (IC 32-31-3-18).
  • Flood plain. For agreements entered into or renewed after June 30, 2009, the rental agreement must say so if the lowest floor, including any basement, is at or below the 100-year flood elevation (IC 32-31-1-21).
  • Military installation. A separate section covers disclosure of property near a military installation (IC 32-31-1-21.1).

A landlord who skips the manager and agent disclosure becomes the agent of each landlord for receiving legal process and notices, and the tenant can recover reasonable expenses spent finding the required names and addresses. The same chapter has sections on requests for law enforcement or emergency assistance and limits on penalties (IC 32-31-1-22), and on the death or incapacitation of a tenant (IC 32-31-1-23).

sections.h2: Preparing a tenant-occupied house for sale
sections.html:
Gather the paperwork first, then handle notices in the order the statutes expect. A clean file helps any buyer, including an investor who plans to keep the tenants.

  • Pull the signed lease, every renewal and any written changes to the rental agreement.
  • Confirm that the manager and agent disclosure was given and update it for the new owner.
  • Check the flood plain status and whether the lease says so where the statute requires.
  • Set showing dates with written notice and keep copies.
  • Decide whether tenants stay or leave, and count the notice periods in the table above if they will leave.
  • Write down each deposit, the date it was paid, and the tenant's mailing address.

Free help exists for tenants and sometimes for small landlords. Indiana Legal Help (indianalegalhelp.org) lets people search for legal aid by county or ZIP code. Indiana Legal Services runs an intake line at 1-844-243-8570, Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., and the state courts keep housing resources at in.gov/courts/housing. Check current hours before you call.

faqs.q: How much notice does a landlord give for unpaid rent?
faqs.a: At least ten days. The tenant can stop the termination by paying in full before the notice period ends, unless the parties agreed otherwise. If the tenant does not pay, the landlord still has to file a court case to evict.

faqs.q: Can a landlord change the locks to get a tenant out?
faqs.a: No. IC 32-31-5-6 bars blocking a tenant's access or possession without a court order and lists changing locks and removing doors or appliances. Shutting off essential services is also barred, except in emergencies or for good-faith repairs and necessary construction.

faqs.q: Does a tenant have to leave when the landlord sells the house?
faqs.a: Not just because of the sale. The conveyance is valid without the tenant's agreement under IC 32-31-1-10, but the lease and the notice rules still control when a tenancy ends.

faqs.q: Can a landlord enter the unit to show it to buyers?
faqs.a: Yes, with reasonable notice at reasonable times. The tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for showings. An emergency allows entry without notice, and a landlord cannot use entry to harass a tenant.

faqs.q: What is the small claims limit for rent and damages?
faqs.a: The limit is $10,000 for the damages hearing in an eviction case.
